title: Autofluorescence Imaging to Evaluate Cellular Metabolism
protocol: Aspirate the medium from an 80-90% confluent T-75 flask of MCF-7 cells.
Rinse the cells with 10 mL of sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS).
Add 2 mL of 0.25% trypsin to detach the cells from the flask bottom.
Incubate the flask at 37 °C for ~4 min.
Check the cells under the microscope to confirm detachment.
Immediately add 8 mL of culture medium to de-activate the trypsin.
Collect the cells in a conical tube (15 mL or 50 mL).
Count the cells using a hemocytometer.
Centrifuge the cells at 200 × g for 5 min.
Aspirate the supernatant once centrifuged.
Resuspend the pellet of cells in 1 mL of culture medium.
Seed 4 × 10^5 cells onto a 35 mm glass-bottom imaging dish.
Add 2 mL of culture medium to the imaging dish to maintain cell metabolism.
Incubate the cells at 37 °C with 5% CO2 for 24-48 h prior to imaging.
Turn on all components of the multiphoton fluorescence lifetime microscope, including the microscope, the laser source, and the detectors being used.
Turn on the brightfield lamp.
Ensure that light is going into the eyepiece.
Choose an objective, usually 20x, 40x, or 100x for cell imaging.
Apply 1 drop of the appropriate immersion medium on top of the objective [skip if using an air objective].
Move the objective down to properly place the sample without touching the objective.
Place the glass-bottom dish onto the sample holder on the microscope stage.
Ensure that the specimen is secure and will not move during imaging.
Center the specimen with the objective using the X-Y stage control.
Look into the eyepiece and move the objective up to focus on the cells.
If the microscope is within an enclosure, close the lightbox door.
Open the image acquisition software.
Click on the Multiphoton Imaging tab.

Set the following multiphoton imaging parameters: image size = 256 x 256 pixels; pixel dwell time = 4-25 µs; total image acquisition time = ~60 s; optimized detector gain for single-photon counting = 85% (specific to the system being used).
Place urea crystals on a glass-bottom dish and secure the dish lid with tape or parafilm.
Image the urea crystals.
Place the urea dish on the microscope stage and focus on a urea crystal.
Set the wavelength of the excitation laser to 900 nm.
Use an emission filter that captures 450 nm wavelengths.
Create a YG bead slide by diluting the YG bead solution 1:1,000 in sterile water.
Place approximately 30 µL of the diluted YG bead solution onto a slide or glass-bottom dish.
Cover with a coverslip and seal the edges of the coverslip with clear nail polish.
Set the wavelength of the excitation laser to 890 nm.
Use an emission filter that captures ~500-600 nm wavelengths.
Obtain a fluorescence lifetime image of the YG bead using a laser power at the sample <1 mW and the recommended image parameters.
Check the lifetime of the bead using the IRF of the urea.
Place the glass-bottom dish with the cells on the microscope stage and focus on the cells.
Place cells in an environmental chamber to maintain heat, humidity, and CO2 levels during image acquisition.
Adjust the gain of the detector to the optimal value for FLIM.
Change to the desired dwell time indicating the time the laser spends at each pixel of the specimen.
Set the multiphoton laser to 750 nm.
Ensure that the power control for the laser is set at zero initially to prevent damage to cells upon opening the shutter on the laser.
Wear appropriate personal protective equipment.
Increase the laser power to ~3-8 mW at the sample while ensuring the cells remain in focus.
Record the maximum laser power used.
Use this recorded power setting for imaging other segments of the Petri dish for NAD(P)H imaging.
Measure the laser power at the sample or pick-off window, not relying on pockels cell voltage.
Collect an NAD(P)H FLIM image with an image integration time of 60 seconds.
Check that the image has sufficient photons (peak of ~100 photons for a cytoplasm pixel).
If photon number is too low, increase laser power or duration of image acquisition.
Set the multiphoton laser to 890 nm and wait for it to mode-lock at the new wavelength.
Ensure the power control for the laser is set at zero initially before opening the shutter.
Do not move the stage or objective focus when conducting this step.
Set an emission filter to collect emission wavelengths at ~500-600 nm.
Begin imaging in a focusing or live-view manner to optimize image settings.
Increase the laser power to ~5-10 mW at the sample and record the maximum power used.
Collect an FAD FLIM image with an image integration time of 60 s.
Check that the image has sufficient photons (peak of ~100 photons for a cytoplasm pixel) within the fluorescence lifetime decay curve.
Increase laser power or duration of image acquisition if photon number is too low.
Repeat steps for four to five FOVs, ensuring each image is spaced at least 2 FOVs away from imaged locations.
Dissolve 130.24 mg of sodium cyanide in 25 mL of PBS to make an 80 mM (20x) sodium cyanide solution.
Aspirate 100 µL of culture medium from the dish.
Replace this with 100 µL of sodium cyanide solution to obtain a 4 mM concentration of cyanide in the dish.
Put the cells in an incubator for 5 min to allow the cells to react with the cyanide solution.
Open the FLIM lifetime analysis software.
Open the urea image to acquire the measured IRF.
Import the urea image into the software.
Select a point on the image of the urea crystal to be used for image analysis.
Increase the spatial bin value to integrate FLIM data from multiple pixels to 1 or higher for a decay peak > 100 photons by changing the Bin variable located on the main software interface.
Save the data as an IRF.
Click the dropdown menu titled IRF, select Copy from Decay Data in the referenced software.
Click Copy to Clipboard to be utilized in the image analysis of the image taken during the experiment.
Import the image file into fluorescence lifetime analysis software for NAD(P)H and FAD lifetime images.
Improve image visualization to see the cells and subcellular compartments by changing the intensity and contrast if needed.
Click the Options dropdown menu and select Intensity.
Change the intensity and contrast as desired and click Ok.
Import the IRF from the urea image.
Click the IRF dropdown menu and select Paste from Clipboard.
Set Multiexponential Decay parameters50.
Set a threshold value to evaluate decays for cytoplasm pixels.
Check that the Shift value aligns the IRF relative to the rising edge of the fluorescence.
Adjust the shift if needed to minimize the Chi-squared value.
Increase the spatial bin so that cytoplasm pixels have fluorescence peak values at or above 100.
Compute fluorescence lifetimes for all pixels in the image.
Click the Calculate dropdown menu | Decay Matrix.
Save the fluorescence lifetime data.
Click the File dropdown menu | Export.
Choose the desired parameters for analysis and click Ok.
Select the Color button from the Options dropdown menu.
Adjust the fluorescence lifetime metric displayed to B-G-R color configuration.
Set specific color bar minimum and maximum values to adjust the color scale of the fluorescence lifetime image.
Download the MCF7_Segmentation_Final.cpproj file.
Import the MCF7_Segmentation Pipeline by clicking on File | Import | Pipeline from file, then select the downloaded file.
Add NAD(P)H intensity images in .tif, .png, or .jpg format to the Images module.
Press Analyze Images button located at the bottom left.
Click Start Test Mode.
Run each module by clicking the play button next to the module name.
Adjust the Typical diameter of objects (Min, Max) for MCF-7 cells to 10 and 40 pixels respectively.
Adjust the Feature size in EnhanceOrSuppressFeatures module to 10 pixels for MCF-7 cells.
Adjust the Range of hole sizes in the second EnhanceOrSuppressFeatures module to 5-20 for MCF-7 cells.

Adjust parameters (Threshold strategy, Thresholding method, Threshold smoothing scale, and Threshold correction factor) in the second IdentifyPrimaryObjects module for optimal identification of nuclei.
Apply identified optimal settings from IdentifyPrimaryObjects module to the IdentifySecondaryObjects module.
Adjust the area shape in FilterObjects module with a minimum pixel value of 100 and maximum pixel value of 500.
Average the fluorescence lifetime output variables for each cell within the image using the cell cytoplasm masks.
Turn on the equipment that will be used during the experiment.
Ensure that the microscope to be used has an appropriate excitation source for NAD(P)H (single-photon wavelength ~370-405 nm: two-photon wavelength ~700-750 nm).
Ensure that the microscope to be used has an appropriate excitation source for FAD (single-photon wavelength ~488 nm, two-photon wavelength ~890 nm).
Ensure that the microscope has a filter for the isolation of NAD(P)H emission (~400-500 nm).
Ensure that the microscope has a filter for isolation of FAD emission (~500-600 nm).
Turn on the brightfield lamp.
Apply 1 drop of the appropriate immersion medium on top of the corresponding objective if needed.
Move the objective down to properly place the samples without any interference.
Place the Petri dish onto the stage properly.
Ensure that the specimen is secure and will not move during imaging.
Center the specimen with the objective.
Look into the eyepiece and move the objective until the cells appear to be in focus.
Open up the imaging software and set the excitation and emission configuration to capture NAD(P)H.
Optimize excitation illumination and detector parameters.
Reduce illumination intensity if bleaching occurs, increase image integration time.
Acquire an NAD(P)H image of desired size.
Save the acquired NAD(P)H image.
Set excitation and emission configuration for FAD imaging.
Optimize excitation illumination and detector parameters again.
Acquire an FAD image.
Ensure the FAD image is saved.
Repeat imaging process at five additional locations, spaced at least 2 FOVs apart.
Open NAD(P)H and FAD intensity images in image processing software.
Set a threshold on NAD(P)H to retain cytoplasm pixels, set background and nucleus pixels to 0.
Calculate the redox ratio image using equation FAD/(NAD(P)H+FAD).
Calculate mean value of non-0 pixels.
Obtain a mask image of cells within each NAD(P)H image.
Calculate the redox ratio image by evaluating the equation FAD/(NAD(P)H+FAD) at each pixel.
Using the cell cytoplasm mask, average the redox ratio for all pixels for each cell within the image.
